cases.note: Spec worked example 1. Exact name with an SH01 36 days before the seed and an office in Leeds. The prefix match is not considered.
Spec worked example 2. A short brand name matching an old company with dormant accounts that end before the round. No signal.
Spec worked example 3. The only exact match was incorporated after the first event.
Spec worked example 4. The grant participant's postcode is the registered office postcode.
Spec worked example 5. No exact match; the platform company has both the location and the filing. Labelled as that company, but D61 sends prefix matches to review, so this counts against recall.
Spec worked example 6. The number is already linked to another company with the same name written with a space. A merge candidate, not a link.
Same name, but the registry company is an old consultancy in Cheltenham, 140 km from the startup's town, with no allotment near the round.
Two exact matches once 'Technologies' is removed. The second has the allotment and a Manchester office and is the right one, but several exact candidates always go to review.
A dissolved company held the name until 2019. The name was reused by a new company in 2024, which has an allotment before the seed.
The only exact match was dissolved six years before the round.
The D61 example. A trading-name prefix match with the location only.
A trading-name prefix match with both the location and an allotment before the round. Labelled as linked, because a careful person would be sure; D61 sends it to review, so it counts against recall.
The exact match is an old company in Guildford, 42 km away. The holdings company in London has the allotment, but an exact candidate decides, and it has no signal.
Dormant accounts for the year that holds the round: a company that allotted shares for cash is not dormant.
Dormant until the year before the round, which is normal for a company formed ahead of its first raise. Allotment 21 days before the seed.
Incorporated during the month of the first (month-precision) event. That is not 'too young': the event may have been late in the month.
News says founded 2021; the exact match was incorporated in 2015. Even with an allotment, a careful person would not be sure.
News founded year one year after incorporation: within the tolerance. Allotment 19 days before the round.
The namesake is registered at a Manchester accountant's address shared by many companies. Without the shared-address check, location would wrongly support it.
A Leeds startup registered at a London formation agent. The location does not count, but the allotment does.
Two SignalFeed companies want one number: another company is already linked to it. This one, matched by its alias, becomes a merge candidate.
The company was renamed. Its previous name matches exactly, and an allotment falls 21 days before the round.
A previous name that only starts with the company's name. Previous names count for exact matches only.
A Scottish (SC) number with an allotment and an Edinburgh office.
A Northern Irish (NI) number. BT districts have no open centroid, so location cannot help; the allotment can.
A Northern Irish company with no allotment near the round. Location cannot be checked in BT districts, so it goes to review.
'Limited' in the news and the registry: a two-word name with the office in the same town and no allotment yet.
An ampersand in the news name and 'AND' in the registry.
A hyphen in the news name ('Re-Frame Labs') and none in the registry ('REFRAME LABS LTD').
A short common brand name. ATLAS LTD has a London office, but it is an old unrelated firm. Location alone does not link a single-word name.
A short name with two exact matches once 'Technologies' is removed. Both go to review.
The company re-registered: the old company was dissolved in 2023 and a new one with the same name was formed before the first round.
Re-registered between rounds: the old company closed before the latest round and the new one was formed after the first. Neither fits all the news, so nothing links.
Step 0: the grant record gives the number (without its leading zero) and the profile name matches.
The grant number's profile has another name. The exact search match has an allotment, but while the grant names a different number nothing links automatically.
Step 0 with a renamed company: the grant name is the profile's previous name.
The exact match is a company limited by guarantee (a charity) while the startup raised a seed round.
A guarantee company is allowed for a grant-only company. The grant postcode is the office postcode.
A US company with a London office. The exact UK match is its subsidiary, a different legal entity, so it goes to review.
The maintainer rejected this number for the company before. It is never proposed again.
'UK' is not stripped: FERNGROVE UK LTD is a prefix match, probably a subsidiary. Review even with both signals.
The grant participant's postcode is in the same district as the office (CB4), not the same full postcode.
Grant postcode in the same district as an office postcode flagged as shared. A shared office counts only on a full postcode match, so this goes to review.
The office is in Guildford, 37 km from Reading: outside the 25 km limit. No allotment.
A distinctive two-word name with the office in the same city and no allotment yet. Location supports it.
The only allotment was 190 days before the round, outside the window. No location.
Allotment exactly 30 days after the round: the edge of the window.
Allotment 31 days after the round: just outside the window. No location.
The round is known only to the year, too vague for the filing window. No location.
Only a debt round: an allotment near it is not support, because the rules count equity rounds only.
The name normalises to two characters, so the company is not searched.
The company was dissolved after its only round. That is not a conflict: it closed later.
The exact match was dissolved years ago. A prefix match has location and an allotment, but it is a film studio that happened to allot shares. Prefix matches go to review.
The registry name matches the company's alias, not its short news name.
The exact-name trading company in London and a holdings company that issued the shares. The exact match decides, by location.
Five prefix matches for a short name. At most three go to review.
D62. No country stated; searched because the round is in GBP. The rules are unchanged: an exact name with an SH01 40 days before the round links.
D62. No country stated; searched because UKTN reported it. Only a prefix match exists, with an SH01 in the window. Prefix matches go to review (D61), and a hint never changes that.
D62. No country stated; a US company raising in USD but reported by UKTN. An unrelated UK company has the exact name and no SH01 near the round. No signal, so review, never a link.
D62. No country stated; searched because the extraction names Bristol. The only exact match was incorporated after the first event, so nothing is linked or proposed.
Spec section 8.3 worked example. First sale 44 days before the round, amounts 2.2% apart.
An amendment from a CIK already linked to a company: that company owns it, whatever the name.
A US issuer with the same name as a UK company. A known country other than US conflicts.
The only name match is already linked to another CIK.
Confirmation case C5: the Form D is a different, smaller offering (85% apart). Not linked; a round within 365 days makes a candidate.
A common single-word name and a news round with no amount. The dates fit, but a real-estate 'Atlas LLC' could file at any time: review.
A single-word name, but the amounts were compared and agree (3.3% apart).
Two non-merged companies share the issuer's name. Nothing is linked.
The name matches, but the company has no funding round near the filing.
The first sale has yet to occur, so the filing cannot confirm. A round within 365 days makes a candidate.
News says founded 2015; the issuer reports incorporation in 2024. A newly formed namesake.
Confirmation case C4: the amount agrees with the total offering, not the amount sold so far.
